ENT Clinical Note – John Doe, DOB 11 / 17 / 1991

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  • Recent insect sting (bee/wasp; patient uncertain which) to right arm “a few minutes ago.”
  • Concern about possible allergic reaction.
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  • Immediate localized redness/rash at sting site.
  • Within minutes patient noted mild breathing difficulty and subjective “weird” sensation of tongue; mild right-sided lip discomfort without obvious swelling; anxiety about progression. No worsening reported during call.
- ENT symptoms:
  • Throat swelling/closure sensation: denies.
  • Voice change/hoarseness: denies.
  • Dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling: denies.
  • Nasal/ocular symptoms: none reported.
  • Stridor/noisy breathing: none.
  • Dyspnea: mild subjective; able to speak full sentences.
  • Swelling distribution: patient perceives mild right lip swelling; doctor observed none. Tongue “feels weird,” no visible swelling on exam.
  • Ear/neck symptoms: none.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  • No prior anaphylaxis; never prescribed epinephrine auto-injector.
  • No previous significant reactions to insect stings noted.
- Allergies and current medications:
  • Allergy: penicillin.
  • Current meds: none; has not yet taken antihistamine.
- Social context:
  • Lives alone; has a cat; speaking from home.

Objective:
- Observable swelling: none of lips or oral cavity on video exam; localized erythematous rash with puncture mark on right arm, no obvious swelling.
- Airway/breathing: breathing comfortable on video; speaking in full sentences.
- Mental status: alert, oriented; mild anxiety.
- Vitals and examination findings: Not recorded.
- Another person present: none.

Assessment:
- Localized allergic reaction to insect sting; low suspicion for systemic/anaphylactic reaction at time of review (trigger identified, no progressive airway compromise, normal exam). Anxiety contributing to symptom perception.

Plan:
- Pharmacologic:
  • Start oral antihistamine – e.g., chlorphenamine (Piriton) 4 mg, dose/route/frequency discussed as “one tablet up to 6×/day,” or alternative once-daily non-sedating antihistamine (exact brand per patient preference). Dose/route/frequency reiterated as not otherwise documented.
- Monitoring / escalation instructions:
  • Seek immediate emergency care (call 999 / attend A&E) if any of the following develop: lip/tongue/facial swelling, throat tightness, voice change, stridor, worsening breathing difficulty, dizziness/collapse, rapidly spreading rash.
  • If localized redness spreads, becomes hot, or painful, arrange re-assessment for possible antibiotic.
- Education:
  • Provided link on recognition of anaphylaxis.
  • Reassured that severe reactions usually occur rapidly; current presentation consistent with localized reaction.
  • Lower threshold to contact GP service if concerns persist or recur.
- Follow-up:
  • No routine ENT/allergy referral at this time; consider if recurrent reactions or unexplained rashes occur.
  • Return to service or A&E as above.

Quality checks (document_quality):
• Missing/expected data: objective vitals (HR, BP, RR, SpO₂), detailed airway assessment (uvular/tongue edema), past use/availability of epinephrine auto-injector, baseline respiratory history, detailed medication list.
• Internal conflicts: patient subjectively feels mild lip swelling vs. clinician observes none (conflict noted).
• Transcript quality: clear audio; minor conversational fillers; no inaudible sections.
